steps.title: Everything from unit 10, together
steps.html:
1 — The tense moves back. After a past reporting verb: present → past, past and present perfect → past perfect, will → would, can → could, must → had to. After a present reporting verb (she says, the article claims) nothing moves.

2 — Questions become statements. No inversion, no do, no question mark; if or whether for yes/no questions.

3 — The verb carries your judgement. Said is neutral; claimed marks a missing proof; admitted marks a concession; denied marks an accusation; pointed out marks a correction; insisted marks resistance. Remember the patterns: admit, deny, suggest and report take -ing or that and never an infinitive; tell, assure, remind and inform need a person.

4 — Hedges do in one word what a source does in five. Apparently and supposedly in speech; reportedly, allegedly and it is thought that in writing. Use allegedly only where a crime is alleged and unproved.

5 — Retelling has its own frame. Open with the hook (Did you read about the man who…?), give the surprising fact, hedge what you cannot support, then say what the point is (What’s amazing about it is that…). That last move is what separates a story from a fact.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• Retelling with no hedge at all, so every claim becomes yours.
  • According to me instead of in my view.
  • Forgetting the backshift in the middle of a long retelling.
  • He denied to run it — no infinitive after deny.
  • Allegedly used for anything merely uncertain.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
The question is usually asked as though the answer were obviously no, but the useful version is narrower: what would have to be true of a story before it deserved to be repeated? My position is that the test is not the source but the chain — how many people the claim passed through, and whether any of them could have checked it.

The case for scepticism is strong. A story goes viral because it is simple enough to retell, and the events that matter are almost always complex; a conflict of nine years arrives as eleven seconds of film. The dominant version of an event is therefore the fastest one, not the most accurate, and the majority of people who share a link have not opened it. Corrections exist, but they reach a small fraction of the original audience. That is the real waste: not the attention, but the suffering that is turned into content and then left uncorrected.

The argument on the other side deserves more respect than it usually gets. Much of what is published online is checked, and some of it is checked better than print ever was, because a mistake is visible to everybody immediately. Speed is not only a weakness: in an emergency, a warning that arrives in four minutes and is seventy per cent right may save more people than a report that arrives in four hours and is complete.

My conclusion is therefore conditional. A claim is worth repeating when it names a source that could be wrong in public, and worth hedging when it does not. Where a person is named as a villain, the standard should be higher still, because an innocent person cannot be un-named. Believing nothing is not scepticism; it is the same laziness as believing everything, and it costs less.
